title: Road to 5 Million Tokens: Breaking Barriers in Long Context Training — Max Ryabinin, Together AI
talk_summary: Max Ryabinin describes Together AI's stack of memory-saving techniques for training transformers at 3-5M token context: FSDP, context parallelism, activation checkpointing, CPU offload, sequence tiling, and U-Pipe buffer reuse. The talk is training-infra specific, but its general mechanisms—profile bottlenecks, chunk work, recompute/offload cold state, reuse buffers—can be adapted to long agent runs.

takeaways.technique: Chunk long sequences instead of materializing full buffers
takeaways.what_they_do: They tile element-wise computations, loss, and MLP work across the sequence length so the system never allocates a huge tensor along the full context dimension.
takeaways.evidence_quote: all the loss computations, all the MLPs, they can be chunked to avoid creating these huge buffers
takeaways.numbers: Stacking techniques makes 3M-token training possible on an 8xH100 node.

takeaways.what_they_do: They recompute activations during the backward pass instead of storing all of them, trading extra compute for lower peak memory.
takeaways.numbers: Activation usage drops by a further factor of eight.

takeaways.technique: Offload cold state and prefetch when needed
takeaways.what_they_do: They store transformer-block inputs off GPU to CPU when not required and prefetch them back before the corresponding backward step.
takeaways.evidence_quote: offload them to CPU when they are not required ... prefetch when you are trying to backpropagate
takeaways.numbers: They cite getting next to 37 GB of data offloaded.

takeaways.technique: Shard heavy work across workers by independent slices
takeaways.what_they_do: They split attention heads across GPUs while each GPU still computes over the full sequence, then aggregate results.
takeaways.evidence_quote: one GPU is only responsible for one attention head here, but it's still computing the attention over the whole sequence
takeaways.numbers: Ulysses context parallelism drops utilization by approximately 8x as expected.

takeaways.what_they_do: They use profiling tools to locate where memory and compute actually go rather than guessing from the architecture.
takeaways.evidence_quote: bottlenecks might appear where you least expect. So, tooling like the PyTorch profiler ... can help you a lot

takeaways.technique: Reuse a smaller scratch buffer across iterations
takeaways.what_they_do: They allocate a smaller buffer and reuse it across multiple head-computation iterations instead of allocating one huge buffer.
takeaways.evidence_quote: allocate a buffer which is smaller, but you reuse it across like two or more different iterations
takeaways.numbers: This helps scale to 5M tokens while matching memory-optimized implementations at 8B and 32B scale.
